core: What a carbon footprint is: total greenhouse-gas emissions caused directly and indirectly by a person, product, organization, or activity, expressed in carbon-dioxide equivalent (CO2e)
The GHG Protocol scopes for organizations: Scope 1 (direct), Scope 2 (purchased electricity/steam/heat/cooling), Scope 3 (other value-chain/indirect, 15 categories, often the largest)
Individual vs organizational vs product footprints and how the boundary is drawn
Carbon offsets and their real limits (additionality, permanence, verification, leakage, double counting)
The history of the individual 'carbon footprint' framing and its promotion by the fossil-fuel industry, without dismissing personal action
A small worked example computing a footprint in CO2e from home electricity use and an emissions factor
supporting: The difference between offsets and renewable energy certificates (RECs)
How emissions factors (e.g., EPA eGRID) turn activity data into CO2e
Generation vs delivered electricity and transmission/distribution losses

claims.claim: A carbon footprint is the total greenhouse-gas emissions caused directly and indirectly by a person, product, organization, or activity, conventionally expressed in carbon-dioxide equivalent (CO2e).
Under the GHG Protocol, Scope 1 emissions are direct GHG emissions from sources owned or controlled by the organization (e.g., fuel combustion in boilers, furnaces, company vehicles).
Scope 2 emissions are indirect emissions associated with the purchase of electricity, steam, heat, or cooling that is consumed by the organization but generated elsewhere.

Scope 3 covers other indirect value-chain emissions and is divided into 15 categories, 8 upstream (purchased goods and services; capital goods; fuel- and energy-related activities; upstream transportation and distribution; waste generated in operations; business travel; employee commuting; upstream leased assets) and 7 downstream (downstream transportation and distribution; processing of sold products; use of sold products; end-of-life treatment of sold products; downstream leased assets; franchises; investments).
The GHG Protocol scopes exist so that direct and indirect emissions are tracked in separate ledgers and so that two or more organizations do not count the same emissions in the same scope.

The EPA eGRID2022 national average carbon-dioxide output rate for electricity generated in 2022 was 823.1 lb CO2 per MWh (about 0.373 kg CO2/kWh), rising to about 867.5 lb CO2 per MWh for delivered electricity after assumed transmission and distribution losses of 5.12%.

A worked illustrative footprint: a U.S. home using about 10,500 kWh of electricity in a year, at the eGRID2022 generation factor of 0.373 kg CO2/kWh, produces about 3,916 kg CO2 (roughly 3.9 metric tons); using the delivered factor (~0.393 kg CO2/kWh) it is about 4.1 metric tons.

A credible carbon offset must be additional (beyond business-as-usual, tested by legal/regulatory, financial, barriers, common-practice, and performance tests), and the resulting reductions must be real, permanent, verified, and enforceable.

Offsets and renewable energy certificates (RECs) are fundamentally different instruments: offsets are measured in metric tons of CO2e from projects that avoid or reduce emissions and are subtracted from an organization's emissions, while RECs are measured in MWh of renewable generation and only affect market-based Scope 2 accounting.

Permanence and leakage are recognized offset-integrity risks: sequestered carbon can be re-released (by logging, fire, drought), and a reduction in one place can shift the emitting activity elsewhere rather than eliminate it.

Journalistic and academic investigations report that BP heavily promoted the individual 'carbon footprint' idea during its 2004-2006 'Beyond Petroleum' campaign (with the ad agency Ogilvy & Mather and spending over $100 million per year), deploying one of the first online personal carbon calculators, which drew close to a quarter-million users in its first year; researchers such as Geoffrey Supran argue this shifted attention toward individual responsibility. BP disputes that it originated the concept.
The term 'carbon footprint' rose to prominence in the mid-2000s and was named an Oxford word of the year in 2007.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether BP 'invented' the carbon footprint concept.
positions: Researchers (e.g., Geoffrey Supran) and journalists say BP popularized the individual-footprint framing through its mid-2000s campaign and early calculator, with the effect of deflecting responsibility onto consumers.
BP responds that NGOs, governments, and news organizations had already popularized carbon calculators before BP offered one around 2005.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the well-documented facts (BP's large campaign and early calculator, the individual-responsibility framing) and attributes the interpretive claim to its proponents while noting BP's dispute, rather than asserting BP coined the term. Personal action is not dismissed.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which electricity emissions factor to use for a footprint.
positions: Generation factor (823.1 lb CO2/MWh, ~0.373 kg/kWh) reflects emissions where power is made.
Delivered factor (867.5 lb CO2/MWh, ~0.393 kg/kWh) adds transmission and distribution losses and better reflects a consumer's share.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The worked example uses the generation factor for the headline number and notes the delivered factor as an alternative, both labeled illustrative and dated to eGRID2022 (EPA 2024).

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained only generic placeholder text ('Carbon Footprints is a foundational concept ... this lesson introduces its meaning') with no substantive, sourced claims about carbon footprints, scopes, offsets, or emissions factors.
